title: Exxon Mobil's Next Earnings Report on July 31 Could Send the Stock Soaring. Here's Why. - The Globe and Mail
content: ExxonMobil has already provided a preliminary glimpse at its second-quarter financial results. They should show a strong improvement over the first quarter, driven by higher oil prices. While near-term oil price volatility can affect its stock, Exxon's strategy is to improve its ability to profit at lower prices. ExxonMobil(NYSE:XOM) plans to release its second-quarter financial results before the market opens on Friday, July 31. The oil giant has already hinted that it will report windfall profits during the period, driven by the war-fueled surge in oil prices. Here’s a look at what to expect when ExxonMobil reports earnings later this week and why the report could send the oil stock soaring. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » ExxonMobil reported its first-quarter financial results in early May. The oil giant delivered mixed results. While it beat analysts' expectations ($1.16 per share of adjusted earnings compared to the $1.00 consensus estimate), its net income declined significantly despite higher oil prices. The company posted $4.2 billion of profits, its lowest level since the first quarter of 2021, down from $6.5 billion in the fourth quarter. The culprit was war-driven supply disruptions, which prevented Exxon from settling financial hedges with the associated physical shipments. This unfavorable timing effect cost it $3.9 billion during the quarter. However, the company expected the hedging-related paper losses to unwind over the next few months as supply disruptions in the Middle East eased. ExxonMobil provided investors with a preliminary glimpse at its second-quarter financial results earlier this month. It indicated that its second-quarter earnings should be about $5 billion higher than the first quarter, driven by higher oil prices and improving refining margins. The company expects its upstream earnings to rise by about $1.6 billion at the midpoint, driven by improved production and strong oil prices (the global oil benchmark Brent averaged $96.68 per barrel, up 23% compared to the first quarter). Meanwhile, its refining earnings could grow by about $2.6 billion, driven by timing effects. While the company will likely continue to face some timing impacts due to ongoing Persian Gulf supply disruptions and higher oil prices, the unwinding of prior timing impacts should significantly boost its second-quarter earnings. Meanwhile, the company’s adjusted earnings should be even stronger. Analysts expect Exxon to report $15.7 billion of adjusted earnings during the second quarter, nearly double the first-quarter’s level. ExxonMobil should report strong second-quarter results this week. That should give its stock the fuel to soar. However, there’s just one potential wrinkle: oil prices. Crude has been extremely volatile this year. Brent oil was over $100 a barrel earlier this week after the U.S. and Iran resumed fighting. But it has cooled off considerably after the fighting stopped, and was recently around $85 a barrel. Oil could continue falling if there’s a peace deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, or it could rally sharply if fighting resumes. That near-term volatility aside, ExxonMobil can thrive in the long term either way. The oil giant is in the middle of a multi-year transformational strategy to bolster profitability, which includes a major structural cost-savings program and heavy investment in developing its advantaged assets (lowest-cost and highest-margin). This strategy will drive double-digit annual earnings and cash flow growth through 2030, assuming the same oil prices and margins as in 2024. Further, it would enable the oil giant to generate $145 billion in cumulative surplus cash at an average Brent price of $65 a barrel. So, even if Exxon stock doesn’t soar after earnings due to lower oil prices, it has the fuel to deliver robust total returns in the coming years at much lower oil prices. That makes it a great long-term investment right now. title: ExxonMobil's Q2 Earnings on Deck: Should You Bet on the Stock? - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM is set to report second-quarter 2026 results on July 31, before the opening bell. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for second-quarter earnings is pegged at $3.87 per share, implying a surge of almost 136% from the year-ago reported number. It has witnessed one downward estimate revision in the past seven days. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for second-quarter revenues is currently pegged at $95.8 billion, suggesting a roughly 18% rise from the year-ago actuals. XOM beat the consensus estimate for earnings in each of the trailing four quarters, with the average surprise being 6.04%. This is depicted in the graph below: Our proven model doesn’t predict an earnings beat for XOM this time around. The combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy), or 3 (Hold) increases the chances of an earnings beat. That isn’t the case here. The leading integrated energy player has an Earnings ESP of -2.40%. XOM currently carries a Zacks Rank #3. You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank stocks here. You can uncover the best stocks to buy or sell before they’re reported with our Earnings ESP Filter. In its latest 8-K SEC filings, XOM stated that it is likely to see a sequential improvement in the June quarter upstream earnings by $3.5 billion to $3.9 billion due to an increase in liquid prices. To have an idea of how oil prices behaved in the June quarter, let's analyze the commodity prices from the data provided by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (“EIA”). The average Cushing, OK, WTI spot prices for April, May and June of this year were $100.32 per barrel, $102.13 per barrel and $84.81 per barrel, respectively, per EIA data. Commodity prices were $63.54 per barrel, $62.17 per barrel and $68.17 per barrel, respectively, in April, May and June of 2025, according to the EIA. A constructive oil-price backdrop due to the Iran war aided the company’s exploration and production businesses in the June quarter of this year, similar to BP plc BP and Chevron Corporation CVX. XOM added that stronger margins from its Energy Products segment are likely to have provided a $2.0 billion to $2.4 billion sequential benefit. XOM's stock has jumped 37.2% over the past year, outperforming the industry’s 35.6% surge. BP has gained 28.4% over the same time frame, while Chevron has rallied 21%. While XOM’s stock price has outperformed the industry, the company appears relatively overvalued. The company's current trailing 12-month enterprise value/earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization (EV/EBITDA) is 10.23x, reflecting that it is trading at a premium compared with the industry average of 6.71x. Both BP and CVX are valued lower at 3.15x and 9.85x, respectively. ExxonMobil has a massive footprint in the Permian, the most prolific oil and gas play in the United States, and offshore Guyana. In the Permian, the integrated giant has been employing lightweight proppant technology and hence is capable of boosting its well recoveries by up to as much as 20%. According to the data from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, the shut-in price for existing wells in the Midland, a sub-basin of the Permian, is $42 per barrel. For Delaware, another sub-basin, the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas estimated the price at $34 per barrel. With West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) crude oil trading above the $80-per-barrel mark, significantly above the shut-in prices, it makes sense for XOM to continue production in the wells. Although the upstream business seems lucrative now, the high oil price is hurting the company’s refining operations, since the input costs have jumped. Also, with a significant proportion of earnings being generated from upstream activities, the company’s business is highly vulnerable to the volatility in commodity prices. Given the backdrop, it might not be wise for investors to bet on the integrated energy giant ahead of earnings because of its overvaluation. However, those who have already invested may hold on to the stock. The AI revolution has already minted millionaires. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM), an integrated energy company operating across crude oil production, natural gas, refining, chemicals, and low-carbon technologies, remains firmly in focus as stronger oil prices renew attention on its future cash-generating capacity. Its scale, diversified operations, and expanding upstream portfolio continue to influence its standing within the S&P 500, while valuation models suggest the current market price may not fully reflect the companys long-term operating strength. ExxonMobils valuation narrative centers on the durability of its free cash flow. The company operates across the energy value chain, allowing upstream production, refining, chemicals, and specialized products to contribute during different commodity cycles. A discounted cash flow approach considers what future cash generation may be worth in present terms. Under this framework, ExxonMobil appears to have room above its current market valuation, provided its major projects continue progressing and operating discipline remains consistent. The valuation case does not depend on unusually rapid expansion. Instead, it rests on stable production, controlled spending, dependable refining operations, and disciplined execution across a broad asset base. That structure can support cash generation even when individual parts of the business face temporary pressure. Firm crude oil prices can improve the economics of ExxonMobils upstream portfolio by supporting revenue and cash flow from producing assets. The effect is particularly important for projects with long operating lives and competitive production costs. However, commodity strength alone does not define the companys outlook. Energy prices can shift sharply in response to supply changes, geopolitical developments, economic conditions, and global consumption patterns. ExxonMobils valuation therefore depends on both the market environment and its ability to maintain efficient operations. As a leading energy stock, the company benefits from geographic diversification and exposure to several parts of the global energy system. This operating breadth provides a more balanced foundation than reliance on a single field, region, or business segment. ExxonMobils offshore operations in Guyana remain a major part of its long-term production strategy. The region has developed into an important source of lower-cost output, supported by large discoveries and a phased development program. Continued progress in Guyana could strengthen production visibility and support future cash generation. The project portfolio also gives ExxonMobil exposure to assets that may remain economically competitive across a range of commodity environments. Large developments still carry important risks. Construction schedules, operating complexity, government policy, environmental oversight, and infrastructure requirements can affect expected returns. The market may therefore apply a degree of caution even when project economics appear attractive. An earnings-based approach also suggests ExxonMobil may be trading below a valuation level supported by its scale and profit profile. This framework compares the market price with the companys earnings capacity while accounting for business quality, operational risk, and sector characteristics. ExxonMobils current earnings multiple appears moderate compared with some large peers, although it remains influenced by the cyclical nature of the oil and gas industry. Energy company earnings can change substantially as crude oil, natural gas, refining margins, and chemical demand move through different phases. The companys integrated structure can soften part of this volatility. Stronger performance in refining or specialty products may provide support when upstream conditions weaken, while favorable commodity prices can lift production earnings during stronger cycles. Future valuation will depend heavily on how ExxonMobil directs capital across major projects, maintenance needs, acquisitions, and emerging energy technologies. Large energy developments require substantial funding before they begin contributing meaningful cash flow. Disciplined project selection can strengthen returns and protect the balance sheet. Poor execution, cost inflation, or delayed production could reduce the value expected from the development pipeline. ExxonMobil has emphasized assets with competitive production costs and long operating lives. This approach may improve resilience during weaker commodity periods while allowing the company to benefit when energy prices remain supportive. Beyond traditional oil and gas activities, ExxonMobil is developing businesses connected to carbon capture, hydrogen, lithium, and lower-emission industrial solutions. These initiatives remain smaller than the companys established operations, but they may create additional long-term opportunities. Their commercial contribution will depend on customer demand, government policy, infrastructure development, and project economics. These businesses should therefore be viewed as strategic options rather than immediate replacements for the companys core energy operations. A successful expansion could broaden ExxonMobils future revenue base and strengthen its role in industrial decarbonization. Weak project economics or uncertain policy support could limit the pace of progress. The valuation picture remains constructive but not without uncertainty. Cash flow models and earnings measures indicate that ExxonMobil may be priced below levels supported by its operating capacity. At the same time, commodity volatility, capital intensity, regulatory pressure, and project execution remain central considerations. The companys future position will depend on reliable production growth, efficient refining operations, disciplined capital allocation, and steady progress across major developments. Strong execution could narrow the gap between current market pricing and estimated intrinsic value, while operational setbacks could keep that valuation gap in place. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM), scale, asset quality, and integrated structure provide a durable foundation. The key question is whether future cash generation can consistently justify the expectations embedded in valuation models. title: Chevron Returns to Iraq: What Do the Latest Oilfield Talks Signal? - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron CorporationCVX is once again exploring opportunities in Iraq, signaling renewed interest in one of the world's largest oil-producing regions. The company recently held discussions with Iraqi officials regarding potential investments in the giant West Qurna 2 and Nassiriya oil fields. This move follows Russia's Lukoil's exit from the West Qurna 2 project, creating an opportunity for Iraq to bring in another international energy major as a potential operator. The latest discussions suggest CVX is evaluating opportunities beyond a single producing asset. In addition to West Qurna 2, the company has signed preliminary agreements to evaluate development opportunities at Nassiriya, which includes four exploration blocks and the Balad oil field. CVX is also expected to participate in technical studies for proposed crude export pipeline projects linking Iraq with Turkey and Syria. Together, these initiatives indicate that Chevron is assessing a broader presence across Iraq's upstream sector and export infrastructure rather than pursuing an isolated investment. The potential opportunity is significant. Iraq possesses some of the world's largest proven crude oil reserves, while fields such as West Qurna 2 rank among the country's highest-producing assets. For CVX, gaining access to these conventional, long-life reservoirs could complement its existing portfolio by adding large-scale production assets capable of generating output for decades. Although the discussions remain preliminary and no final investment decisions have been announced, they underscore Chevron's growing interest in expanding its footprint in the Middle East. Chevron is not alone in recognizing Iraq's long-term potential. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOMestablished its presence through the development of the giant West Qurna 1 field, demonstrating the value international oil companies place on Iraq's low-cost conventional reserves. TotalEnergies SETTE has taken a broader approach through its Gas Growth Integrated Project, combining oil production, natural gas processing, water infrastructure and renewable energy investments. Meanwhile, BPBP recently strengthened its commitment by signing an agreement to redevelop the Kirkuk oil fields, while ConocoPhillips agreed to acquire a 42% interest in the project, reinforcing the industry's continued confidence in Iraq's resource base. Chevron's latest discussions therefore represent more than a return to Iraq — these reflect a potential effort to secure a stronger position in one of the world's most strategically important oil markets. If these preliminary agreements ultimately lead to operating contracts and investment approvals, the company could meaningfully expand its international upstream portfolio while joining other global energy majors that are increasing their investments in Iraq. Over the past year, Chevron's shares appreciated 21.7%, delivering a solid positive return. However, the stock lagged key integrated energy peers, including ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies and BP’s rise of 38.8%, 38.1% and 29.6%, respectively. Chevron's trailing P/E ratio stands at approximately 13.5x, slightly below ExxonMobil's 14x. However, its valuation remains substantially higher than BP's 9.19x and TotalEnergies' 8.61x, suggesting investors are willing to pay a higher multiple for the stock than for those European oil majors. Over the past 60 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for 2026 earnings has decreased 0.89%, while the estimate for 2027 has increased 3.6%. CVX's renewed engagement with Iraq comes at a time when global energy companies are competing for access to large, low-cost, long-life oil reserves. While the company's discussions remain at an early stage, potential investments in West Qurna 2, Nassiriya and export infrastructure could strengthen CVX's international production portfolio and support long-term growth. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) has moved into the market spotlight as crude prices retreated sharply following an easing of tensions in the Middle East over the weekend, a shift that rippled quickly across the energy sector. The pullback in oil came as fears over disruptions to supply eased, sending both global and US crude benchmarks lower and pressuring the shares of the largest producers. For an integrated major like ExxonMobil, whose fortunes are woven into the global price of oil and gas, such swings are part of the terrain. As the new week opens, the market is weighing what the retreat in crude signals for the sector and how the largest producers are positioned to navigate a backdrop where geopolitics can move prices in a matter of hours. The oil and gas sector sits at the foundation of the global economy, supplying the energy that powers transportation, industry, and daily life. It spans a long chain of activity, from the exploration and production of crude and natural gas, through the refining that turns raw hydrocarbons into usable fuels, to the marketing that delivers those products to customers. Prices across this chain are set in global markets that respond to the balance of supply and demand, and that balance can shift quickly in response to economic conditions, production decisions, and geopolitical events. Because energy is so essential and so widely traded, the sector is unusually sensitive to headlines, and a single development in a distant region can move prices around the world. That sensitivity was on full display over the weekend as an easing of tensions sent crude lower. ExxonMobil is an integrated major, meaning it operates across the entire length of the oil and gas chain rather than focusing on a single segment. Its upstream business explores for and produces crude and natural gas from fields around the world, including a substantial position in the prolific basins of North and South America. Its downstream operations refine crude into fuels and lubricants and market those products to customers. And its chemicals arm turns hydrocarbons into the building blocks of countless everyday products, from packaging to automotive components. The company is also pursuing lower-carbon efforts in areas such as carbon capture and hydrogen. This breadth is the defining feature of the integrated model: when crude prices fall, refining and chemicals can sometimes benefit from cheaper feedstock, providing a measure of balance across the cycle. Commentary from the majors emphasized their focus on operating efficiently, keeping costs in check, and distributing capital back to the owners of the business through dividends and capital-distribution programs, all while continuing to spend on their most productive assets. The integrated majors described maintaining their spending plans even as prices fluctuated, a sign of the discipline that has characterized the sector in recent years. That steadiness matters because it allows these companies to weather the swings of the commodity cycle without abandoning the long-term projects that underpin their production, and it has become a central theme in how the majors present themselves to the market. Efficiency means squeezing more production from their assets while keeping expenses in check, a discipline that has become central to how these companies operate. Cost control matters especially in a business where prices are set by global markets beyond any single company's control, since keeping costs low allows a producer to remain resilient even when prices fall. And disciplined capital allocation means directing spending toward the most productive assets while returning surplus cash to the owners of the business. ExxonMobil has framed much of its operational messaging around these themes, emphasizing the durability that comes from operating efficiently across the entire energy chain through the swings of the cycle. This discipline has become a central theme in how the majors present themselves and in how the market judges their resilience. This is why the movements of crude and the reporting from the major producers draw such close attention, offering a read on the global economy that reaches far beyond the oil and gas sector itself.                                        My Trusted Source ExxonMobil has completed its corporate redomiciliation to Texas, a move landing as firmer crude prices and shipping-route disruptions reshape the backdrop for its upstream operations. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) has completed its corporate redomiciliation to Texas, shifting its state of incorporation away from New Jersey in a move that closes out a process the company had signaled for months. The shift lands at a moment when firmer crude prices and disruptions to global shipping routes used by crude and liquefied-gas carriers are lending support to upstream results across the integrated energy space, giving the redomiciliation added resonance beyond the realm of corporate paperwork. The decision to redomicile is more than a symbolic gesture toward the state where ExxonMobil already maintains its operational headquarters in Spring, a suburb of Houston. Texas has, over recent years, positioned itself as a preferred jurisdiction for corporate charters, offering a specialized business court system and statutes that companies have described as more predictable and less prone to prolonged litigation than those found in some other states. ExxonMobil joins a lengthening roster of large public companies that have opted to reincorporate in Texas, a trend that has picked up pace as boards and general counsel offices weigh the comparative advantages of different legal domiciles. For a company of ExxonMobil's scale, the redomiciliation carries practical implications touching corporate governance, the venue for legal disputes, and the framework under which stockholder meetings and votes are conducted. The company has framed the change as consistent with where its workforce, infrastructure, and decision-making already reside, given that Texas has long served as the operational nerve center for its upstream, downstream, and chemical businesses. The move also arrives against a backdrop in which several other prominent energy and industrial names have made similar transitions, reinforcing the sense that Texas is consolidating its standing as a hub not just for physical energy infrastructure but for corporate charters themselves. The redomiciliation news coincides with a period in which crude benchmarks have firmed, a dynamic that matters enormously for a company whose upstream segment remains the single largest driver of overall results. Crude pricing has been shaped by a mix of factors this year, including supply management by major producing nations, demand patterns tied to industrial activity across large economies, and periodic bouts of geopolitical tension that have injected volatility into tanker movements and shipping lanes. Disruptions affecting vessels that carry crude oil and liquefied natural gas through key maritime corridors have added a layer of support to prices, as market participants price in the added cost and complexity of rerouting cargoes or insuring vessels transiting contested waters. These disruptions have periodically affected chokepoints that matter for global energy flows, prompting shippers to adjust routes, extend voyage times, and in some cases pay materially higher insurance premiums. For an integrated major like ExxonMobil, this environment has generally supported the price realizations achieved across its upstream portfolio, even as the downstream and chemical segments continue to navigate their own separate set of margin dynamics tied to refining spreads and petrochemical demand. ExxonMobil's upstream business spans a global footprint that includes the Permian Basin in West Texas and New Mexico, deepwater developments offshore Guyana, assets in the Gulf of Mexico, and a portfolio of international positions spanning multiple continents. The Permian remains a centerpiece of the company's domestic production strategy, with the company continuing to apply advanced drilling and completion techniques to extract barrels efficiently from unconventional formations. Guyana, meanwhile, has emerged as one of the more closely watched growth stories in the global upstream space, with a series of floating production vessels brought online in recent years that have rapidly scaled output from what was, not long ago, a frontier exploration area. The combination of these legacy and newer assets gives ExxonMobil a production base that is more diversified than many of its integrated peers, spreading exposure across onshore unconventional resources, offshore deepwater fields, and a mix of oil-weighted and gas-weighted output. This diversification has helped the company capture upside when crude prices firm while also providing some insulation when individual basins face localized headwinds, whether from weather events, regulatory changes, or infrastructure bottlenecks. Beyond the upstream segment, ExxonMobil operates an extensive downstream refining network and a global chemical manufacturing business that together provide a counterweight to the cyclicality inherent in crude production. Refining margins have fluctuated through the year as global product demand patterns shift, with gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel consumption all subject to seasonal swings and broader economic currents. The chemical segment, which produces feedstocks and derivatives used across packaging, construction, and consumer goods manufacturing, has faced its own set of pressures tied to global industrial demand and competition from new capacity additions in other regions. The integrated model that spans upstream, downstream, and chemicals has long been a defining characteristic of ExxonMobil's structure, distinguishing it from pure-play exploration and production companies that carry more concentrated exposure to crude price swings. This structure allows the company to smooth some of the volatility that would otherwise flow directly to the bottom line when crude prices move sharply in either direction. ExxonMobil operates in a competitive field that includes Chevron (NYSE:CVX), which also maintains a large-scale integrated model spanning upstream production and downstream refining, as well as European majors and a range of independent exploration and production companies with more concentrated regional footprints. Within the domestic natural gas and liquids export space, companies such as Cheniere Energy (NYSE:LNG) have built distinct positions around liquefied natural gas export infrastructure, a segment that has grown in strategic importance as global buyers look to diversify supply sources. The competitive dynamics among these companies play out across several dimensions, including cost of production, access to low-cost resource basins, downstream integration, and the pace at which each company brings new production online. ExxonMobil's scale advantages, drawn from decades of accumulated infrastructure, technical expertise, and balance sheet capacity, have generally allowed it to pursue large, capital-intensive projects that smaller companies would find difficult to finance or execute. The Guyana development, in particular, illustrates this dynamic, representing a scale of offshore capital deployment that few companies beyond the largest integrated majors could realistically undertake. The broader energy sector has continued to navigate a period defined by several intersecting trends. Global demand for crude oil and refined products has remained resilient even as electrification and efficiency gains slowly reshape long-run consumption patterns in some regions. At the same time, natural gas has taken on a growing role both as a power-generation fuel and as an export commodity, with liquefied natural gas cargoes increasingly bridging supply gaps in regions seeking to diversify away from single-source pipeline dependence. Shipping and logistics disruptions have periodically punctuated this backdrop, adding friction to global energy flows and, in turn, supporting prices for both crude oil and liquefied natural gas. These disruptions have underscored the strategic importance of maritime chokepoints and have prompted renewed attention to the resilience of global energy supply chains. For companies like ExxonMobil that maintain global production and shipping footprints, these dynamics require constant operational recalibration, from adjusting tanker nominations to managing insurance and routing decisions in real time. Regulatory and legal environments across different jurisdictions have also become a more prominent consideration for large energy companies, feeding into decisions such as ExxonMobil's redomiciliation. Companies operating across many states and countries must weigh differing tax treatments, permitting timelines, and litigation exposure when deciding where to locate both physical infrastructure and corporate charters. The trend toward Texas incorporation reflects, in part, a broader reassessment among corporate boards of where the balance of predictability, cost, and legal familiarity best serves long-run operational needs. ExxonMobil has emphasized capital discipline in recent years, favoring a portfolio approach that prioritizes lower-cost, higher-margin projects over volume growth for its own sake. This approach has meant selectively advancing developments in the Permian and Guyana while maintaining more measured spending in higher-cost or less economically attractive basins. The company has also pursued a series of acquisitions and portfolio adjustments designed to concentrate its resource base around assets it considers most competitive on a full-cycle cost basis. This discipline extends to how the company allocates cash generated from operations, balancing reinvestment in production capacity against distributions to stockholders through dividends and buyback programs. The approach reflects a broader shift across the integrated energy space, where companies have generally moved away from the aggressive volume-growth strategies that characterized earlier cycles and toward a framework that emphasizes free cash flow generation and capital efficiency. Several operational themes are likely to remain central to how ExxonMobil is evaluated by market participants and industry watchers in the period ahead. Continued ramp-up of production capacity in Guyana, ongoing efficiency gains in the Permian, and the pace of project execution across the company's global portfolio will all factor into how the upstream segment performs. On the downstream side, refining margins tied to seasonal product demand and the broader health of global industrial activity will shape how that segment contributes to overall results. The chemical business, meanwhile, continues to navigate a period of oversupply in certain regions as new manufacturing capacity has come online globally, pressuring margins for commodity-grade products. ExxonMobil has sought to differentiate its chemical portfolio through specialty and performance products that command steadier margins, a strategy shared by several peers navigating similar industry-wide capacity pressures. The developments surrounding ExxonMobil carry relevance well beyond the company itself, touching on broader themes that resonate across the Energy Stocks category. The interplay between firmer crude prices, shipping-route disruptions, and corporate domicile decisions illustrates how operational, market, and legal considerations increasingly intersect for large energy companies. As a constituent of the NYSE Composite, ExxonMobil's performance and strategic decisions are often read as a proxy for broader sentiment toward the traditional energy complex, even as the sector continues to coexist alongside a growing renewable and lower-carbon power generation landscape led by companies such as NextEra Energy (NYSE:NEE). The redomiciliation itself, while primarily a legal and administrative matter, has drawn attention because of the signal it sends about how large energy companies are thinking about long-run corporate structure at a time when the operating environment for crude and natural gas remains dynamic. Whether other major energy companies follow a similar path in the period ahead remains a topic of ongoing discussion among market watchers tracking corporate governance trends across the sector. ExxonMobil's operational presence in Texas has grown substantially over recent years, anchored by its campus north of Houston that consolidated operations previously spread across multiple sites. The redomiciliation formalizes a relationship between the company and the state that has already been deepening through years of infrastructure spending, workforce expansion, and engagement with local and state governments on matters ranging from permitting to workforce development programs tied to the energy and petrochemical industries concentrated along the Gulf Coast. The Gulf Coast region more broadly continues to serve as a critical hub for energy infrastructure, hosting a dense concentration of refining capacity, petrochemical manufacturing, and export terminals that collectively make the region one of the most significant energy corridors globally. ExxonMobil's decision to formalize its corporate home in Texas reinforces the state's centrality to the broader domestic and global energy supply chain, a positioning shared by numerous other companies with significant Gulf Coast operations. Beyond crude oil, natural gas and liquefied natural gas have taken on outsized importance for the broader energy complex, and ExxonMobil maintains meaningful exposure to both through its upstream gas production and its participation in liquefied natural gas export ventures along the Gulf Coast and in other regions internationally. Disruptions affecting liquefied-gas carriers moving through key maritime corridors have added a layer of complexity to global gas flows this year, prompting buyers in Asia and Europe to adjust sourcing patterns and, in some cases, pay elevated prices for cargoes rerouted around affected chokepoints. This dynamic has reinforced the strategic value of flexible, diversified gas supply, a theme that resonates across companies with liquefied natural gas exposure, including Cheniere Energy (NYSE:LNG), which has built its entire commercial model around long-term export contracts tied to global gas demand. ExxonMobil's own gas positions, spanning both domestic unconventional resources and international liquefaction ventures, place it among the handful of companies capable of supplying meaningful incremental volumes to global buyers seeking to diversify away from single-source pipeline dependence, a priority that has only grown more pronounced amid recurring shipping disruptions. ExxonMobil has continued to emphasize technology as a lever for improving well productivity and lowering per-barrel costs across its unconventional and deepwater portfolios. In the Permian, this has meant longer lateral wells, more precise completion designs, and greater use of data analytics to optimize drilling schedules and reduce non-productive time on rigs. These efficiency gains have become an increasingly important differentiator among operators competing for capital and drilling inventory in a basin that has matured considerably since its early growth years. Offshore in Guyana, technology has manifested differently, with the company deploying advanced subsea architecture and floating production vessels engineered to bring new fields online on accelerated timelines compared with historical deepwater project cycles. The pace at which successive vessels have been sanctioned and brought into service reflects a broader industry shift toward standardized, repeatable project designs that shorten the interval between discovery and first output, a capability that has become a meaningful competitive differentiator in the deepwater segment specifically. ExxonMobil has maintained a long-standing record of returning cash to stockholders through both dividends and buyback programs, a practice the company has continued even through periods of commodity price volatility. This approach reflects a broader capital allocation framework that prioritizes steady distributions alongside disciplined reinvestment in the highest-return segments of the portfolio. The balance between funding growth projects such as Guyana and the Permian on one hand, and maintaining consistent stockholder distributions on the other, has remained a central theme in how the company communicates its capital allocation priorities to the broader market. This framework has also shaped how ExxonMobil approaches acquisitions, favoring transactions that add durable, low-cost resource positions rather than pursuing scale for its own sake. The company's approach in this regard mirrors strategies pursued by Chevron (NYSE:CVX) and other integrated peers, all of which have gravitated toward similar capital discipline principles following a period in prior years marked by heavier spending and, at times, lower capital efficiency across the broader upstream sector. The combination of a sharp move in oil and an imminent earnings print has placed the company squarely in focus, since few names are as closely tied to the direction of crude as this integrated giant. The attention reflects the way ExxonMobil sits at the heart of the energy story running through the market. When oil surges on supply fears, the largest producers become the most direct beneficiaries in the eyes of market participants, and the company's scale across exploration, production and refining makes it a natural reference point. With geopolitics keeping crude volatile, the run-up to its report has taken on added weight this week. The immediate trigger is twofold: crude oil pushing above the hundred-dollar mark on Red Sea disruption and Houthi attacks, and ExxonMobil's scheduled earnings report at week's end. The jump in oil prices lifts the value of every barrel the company produces, while the coming print will show how the business is translating a firmer energy backdrop into results across its upstream and downstream operations. The Red Sea disruption matters because it threatens the smooth flow of crude and refined products through a critical maritime corridor, stoking fears of tighter supply. Those fears feed directly into higher prices, and for a producer of ExxonMobil's magnitude, a sustained move in oil can reshape the earning power of the enterprise. That linkage is precisely why the stock has stepped into sharper focus as the week begins. The oil and gas sector spans exploration and production at one end, midstream transport and storage in the middle, and refining and marketing at the other. ExxonMobil is an integrated major, meaning it operates across this entire chain, from pulling crude out of the ground to turning it into fuels and chemicals supplied to end markets. This integration is a defining feature that distinguishes the largest players from pure-play producers. The sector's fortunes swing with the price of crude, which itself responds to the balance of global supply and demand and to geopolitical events like the current Red Sea tensions. When prices climb, upstream producers capture more value per barrel, though refining margins can compress if crude costs outrun fuel prices. ExxonMobil's spread across the chain gives it a degree of natural balance, cushioning some of the swings that buffet narrower operators. ExxonMobil organizes its business around upstream exploration and production, downstream refining and marketing, and a large chemicals arm. The upstream unit develops oil and gas fields across continents and offshore basins, while the downstream network turns crude into gasoline, diesel and other fuels. The chemicals division converts hydrocarbons into plastics and specialty products used across manufacturing. This integrated structure is central to how the company generates and balances its earnings. When crude prices are high, the upstream segment prospers; when they ease, refining and chemicals can pick up some slack. The company has also pursued a portfolio of large developments in prolific basins, aiming to grow output from low-cost barrels while pruning higher-cost assets. This disciplined shaping of the asset base is a recurring theme in how ExxonMobil describes its strategy. The market environment this week is dominated by two forces for the energy group: the surge in crude and the crowded earnings calendar. While megacap technology names and a Federal Reserve rate decision command attention elsewhere, energy majors are being watched through the lens of the oil move, which touches inflation, corporate earnings and the broader mood of the market. Recent sessions have been choppy, with equities closing an unsettled week as geopolitics stayed in focus. Against that backdrop, energy stocks have drawn interest as a hedge against inflation and geopolitical shocks, since higher oil often lifts producer earnings even when other sectors wobble. As a component of the [Dow Jones Industrial Average], ExxonMobil carries weight in a closely watched barometer, so its moves resonate beyond the energy complex. One defining trend is the emphasis on capital discipline across the industry. After earlier cycles of heavy spending, producers have prioritized efficiency, focusing capital on the lowest-cost, highest-yielding barrels and channeling cash to owners of the stock through dividends and cash distributions. ExxonMobil has embraced this discipline, framing measured spending as a way to weather the swings inherent in commodity markets. A second trend is the gradual push toward lower-carbon energy alongside traditional production. Majors are directing capital toward areas such as carbon capture, hydrogen and biofuels, seeking to position for an evolving energy landscape while continuing to supply the oil and gas the world still relies on. ExxonMobil has committed resources to these ventures, framing them as a complement to its core business rather than a replacement, a stance that reflects the sector's careful navigation of the energy transition. ExxonMobil positions itself as a low-cost, integrated producer with the scale and technical expertise to develop complex projects across the globe. Its strategy centers on advantaged assets, meaning fields and facilities that generate strong economics even when prices soften. This positioning is meant to reassure the market that the company can prosper across a range of oil-price environments rather than only when crude is high. The company also emphasizes operational integration as a competitive edge, arguing that owning the full chain from wellhead to end product provides resilience and flexibility. This integrated identity, paired with a focus on capital discipline and selective growth, forms the backbone of how ExxonMobil presents itself. In a moment when crude has surged, that positioning takes on fresh relevance as market participants weigh how fully the company can capture the upswing. Recent developments across the energy majors have centered on how firmly they can capture higher crude prices while maintaining spending discipline. As oil climbs on the Red Sea disruption, attention has turned to whether producers will keep capital budgets restrained or chase growth. ExxonMobil has signaled a preference for measured spending concentrated in its most advantaged assets, a stance market watchers will scrutinize in the coming report. The company has also advanced developments in prolific offshore basins and continued to expand its chemicals and lower-carbon ventures. These moves reflect an effort to grow durable, low-cost output while positioning for a shifting energy mix. Each strand feeds the narrative that greets ExxonMobil as it approaches its earnings print, with the crude surge sharpening interest in how the integrated model is performing right now. Operationally, ExxonMobil concentrates on driving down the cost of producing each barrel while lifting the reliability of its refining and chemicals facilities. The company has pursued efficiency gains through technology, project execution and the high-grading of its portfolio toward its best assets. This relentless focus on cost is meant to widen the margin between what it spends and what it earns, especially valuable when prices swing. At the same time, the company channels capital toward a handful of large growth projects and toward its lower-carbon initiatives, balancing near-term output against longer-horizon positioning. Managing this balance, sustaining production while committing resources to the energy landscape ahead, is a continuing operational theme. ExxonMobil frames the approach as one that preserves flexibility across the commodity cycle while keeping spending firmly under control. The industry faces enduring challenges. The volatility of crude prices means earnings can swing sharply with global supply and demand, testing the discipline of even the largest players. Geopolitical events like the Red Sea disruption can send prices soaring or crashing with little warning, complicating planning. ExxonMobil must navigate this inherent volatility while sustaining long-cycle developments that take years to bear fruit. The energy transition presents another challenge, as pressure mounts to reduce emissions and prepare for a lower-carbon world even while meeting current demand for oil and gas. Balancing spending on traditional production against emerging lower-carbon ventures is a delicate act. Layered onto these are regulatory and environmental demands that vary across the many jurisdictions where the company operates, adding complexity to an already cyclical business. ExxonMobil competes with a handful of other integrated supermajors for the largest and most complex energy projects, alongside national oil companies that control vast reserves and nimble independents focused on specific basins. The rivalry centers on securing advantaged resources, executing projects efficiently and maintaining the financial strength to weather downturns. Scale and technical depth are decisive advantages in this arena. Beyond traditional rivals, the company faces competition tied to the energy transition, as firms across the spectrum position for a lower-carbon landscape. ExxonMobil leans on its integrated model, technical expertise and financial heft to argue that it can both supply today's energy needs and adapt to tomorrow's. That integrated stance underpins how the company frames its standing among Oil and Gas Stocks drawing heightened attention as crude climbs this week. The crude surge is the single most influential variable for a producer of this profile. Higher oil prices lift the value of every barrel ExxonMobil pumps, directly boosting the earning power of its upstream segment. The move above the hundred-dollar mark therefore carries real weight for the coming report, as it frames how strongly the company can capture the upswing across its operations. The Red Sea disruption underpinning the surge also injects uncertainty, since prices could ease if tensions calm or climb further if the situation deteriorates. Refining margins add nuance, as costlier crude can squeeze the downstream unit even as it lifts the upstream. How ExxonMobil balances these cross-currents will shape sentiment toward the stock as its results approach and the energy story continues to unfold this week. While the upstream captures headlines during an oil surge, the refining and chemicals arms play a crucial role in the integrated model. Refining margins hinge on the spread between crude costs and fuel prices, and a rapid climb in oil can compress that spread if pump prices lag. ExxonMobil's downstream network is therefore watched closely for how it navigates the shifting economics of turning crude into products. The chemicals division adds another dimension, converting hydrocarbons into plastics and specialty materials whose demand tracks global manufacturing. This segment can steady results when upstream or refining swings, but it is exposed to industrial cycles and feedstock costs. The interplay among these three arms, upstream, refining and chemicals, is central to how the integrated model performs, and it will feature prominently in the read on the company's results. The relevance of ExxonMobil stretches far beyond its own shares. As one of the world's largest energy producers, its performance shapes sentiment across the entire oil and gas complex and feeds into the broader inflation debate that grips the market. When a surge in crude lifts a major of this scale, the effect ripples through related sectors and colors the mood of the wider market. That barometer function explains why the stock has climbed into focus as crude tops the hundred-dollar mark and results loom this week. ExxonMobil sits at the meeting point of geopolitics, energy prices and inflation, giving its story a reach that touches many corners of the market. For anyone tracking how the oil surge is rippling through the economy, the company offers one of the clearest available vantage points in the days ahead. Beyond crude oil, ExxonMobil maintains a substantial position in natural gas, including liquefied natural gas developments that serve growing demand across Asia and Europe. Natural gas has taken on added prominence as economies seek cleaner-burning fuel to complement the transition toward lower-carbon energy, and the Red Sea disruption has sharpened attention on the security of global energy supply routes. content: U.S. stock futures surged early Monday after reports that the United States and Iran agreed to pause military strikes over the weekend triggered a sharp selloff in crude oil prices. Wall Street gears up for one of the busiest weeks this year, with nearly one-third of S&P 500 companies scheduled to report earnings, including four Magnificent Seven companies: Apple Inc. (AAPL), Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) and Meta Platforms Inc. (META). He also said that the company has used an early form of AI in work with Memorial Sloan Kettering and added that analyzing the genetic makeup of tumors could help speed drug development and improve patient selection. (OTLK) rallied 12% overnight heading into Monday after the FDA approved Lytenava, the company’s eye drug for treating wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), removing a major regulatory hurdle and putting the spotlight on how much value it can capture as it prepares for a U.S. launch. OTLK stock jumped 6% on Friday to $1.41, snapping two straight sessions of losses. Outlook Therapeutics said on Friday that the FDA approved Lytenava for wet AMD, making it the first and only FDA-approved version of Bevacizumab developed specifically for use in the eye. The decision came ahead of the FDA's July 29 target date and marks a major turnaround after several regulatory setbacks. In December 2025, the FDA rejected Outlook's application and asked for more evidence that the drug was effective. Outlook appealed, and in May the FDA's Office of New Drugs ruled that the existing data were sufficient and that no additional clinical trials were needed. That decision allowed Outlook to resubmit its application in June, leading to Friday's approval. Outlook estimates the U.S. market for anti-VEGF retinal treatments at about $8.5 billion annually, with millions of eye injections given each year. Bevacizumab has been used for more than 20 years in retinal care, including for wet AMD, but largely on an off-label basis. Lytenava stands out because it was developed specifically for injection into the eye and is now FDA-approved for wet AMD. Outlook also expects Lytenava to receive 12 years of U.S. market exclusivity under biologics law. The drug is already approved in the European Union and U.K., with commercial launches underway in Germany, Austria and the U.K. Outlook expects Lytenava to become available to eligible U.S. patients before year-end. The company is expanding reimbursement and patient-support access, building a specialized retina commercial organization and supporting physicians as it prepares for rollout. Economist Paul Krugman warned that President Donald Trump's war against Iran has resulted in refining costs soaring, thereby magnifying the economic impact of higher crude prices. In a note published Thursday, the Nobel Prize-winning economist said crude oil prices hovering around $100 a barrel, combined with an unusually wide gasoline refining "crack spread" worth roughly another $40 per barrel, have left the world facing the economic equivalent of $140 per barrel for oil. “Trump’s gratuitous war on Iran has turned into a remarkable quagmire — remarkable because the only thing keeping the war going is Trump’s vanity. He effectively lost the war in the first few days,” Krugman said. The economist’s comments come amid an escalation in tensions between the U.S. and Iran. Trump said on Thursday that he will hold Iran responsible for any subsequent attacks by the Houthi rebels in the Red Sea, after an attack by the group on Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the region earlier this week. He also added that the U.S. will inflict “major military punishment” upon Iran and the Houthis if they attack ships again. Krugman argued that looking at crude oil prices alone understates the economic impact of the conflict. While benchmark crude has climbed to around $100 a barrel, he said the cost of turning crude into gasoline has also surged, with the refining "crack spread" widening to roughly $40 per barrel. Combined, those two components amount to the equivalent of $140 oil, according to Krugman. He said that the large refining margin means consumers are paying far more at the pump than crude prices alone would suggest, making the economic shock significantly more severe despite oil remaining well below historical peaks in nominal terms. The crack spread measures the difference between the price of crude oil and the value of refined products such as gasoline and diesel, serving as a key indicator of refinery profit margins. Crude oil prices eased on Friday after Brent soared past $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May 20, 2026. U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures expiring in September were down 2.97%, hovering around $89.45 a barrel. Brent crude futures expiring in September fell 3.13%, hovering around $97.54 a barrel. The United States Oil Fund ETF (USO) and the ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil ETF (UCO) were down about 2%. Krugman warned that the current energy shock could worsen significantly if the Iran conflict worsens. While he described the present situation as manageable, he said a broader regional war could disrupt energy supplies further and deepen the economic fallout. He also cautioned that any escalation would likely drive up both crude prices and refining margins, amplifying the pressure on consumers and businesses. "Things could get much uglier if this war escalates," Krugman wrote, arguing that the current equivalent of $140 oil may not represent the worst-case scenario. The economist argued that surging energy prices, combined with Trump's new tariffs, could reverse recent progress on inflation and push interest rates higher, intensifying the financial strain on households and businesses. This comes days ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee’s (FOMC) meeting later this month. According to the CME FedWatch tool, the odds of a 25 basis point rate hike during the July meeting are currently at 35.8%, compared to odds of 64.2% that the Fed keeps rates unchanged. title: Nasdaq Futures Lead US Premarket Rally As Iran Ceasefire Reports Ease Fears Ahead Of Big Tech Earnings: Why NVDA, ORCL, SPCX, XOM, OTLK Are In Focus - TradingView
content: U.S. stock futures surged early Monday after reports that the United States and Iran agreed to pause military strikes over the weekend triggered a sharp selloff in crude oil prices. Wall Street gears up for one of the busiest weeks this year, with nearly one-third of S&P 500 companies scheduled to report earnings, including four Magnificent Seven companies: Apple Inc. (AAPL), Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) and Meta Platforms Inc. (META). Investors will also be watching the Federal Reserve’s July policy decision, second-quarter GDP data and the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index later this week. As of 4:00 a.m. ET, Nasdaq futures soared 1.5%, Dow and S&P 500 futures rose 0.9%, and Russell 2000 futures were up 1.2%. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), an exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500 Index, remained ‘extremely bearish,’ while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, has moved to ‘bearish’ from ‘extremely bearish’ last week. Nvidia (NVDA): Rose 1% in early premarket trade after reports revealed it is in talks to provide a $250 billion financing backstop for OpenAI’s 10-gigawatt Ohio data center project. NVDA also announced a $500 billion partnership with SK Group, a $1B investment in South Korea's Naver, and the rollout of its first U.S.-made GB300 chips from TSMC’s Arizona fab. Oracle Corp. (ORCL): Shares saw a 3% relief rally in early premarket trade on Nvidia’s reported $250B OpenAI backstop. Since OpenAI is one of Oracle's largest cloud customers, traders viewed the development as a potential boost to Oracle’s long-term AI infrastructure business. Meanwhile, China's Moonshot AI is reportedly preparing to open-source its Kimi K3 model, renewing debate over whether Chinese AI developers are closing the gap with OpenAI and Anthropic. Alphabet Inc. (GOOGL): In focus after a top executive confirmed memory chip price hikes (up sixfold) will force higher pricing for the upcoming Pixel 11 series. SpaceX (SPCX): Shares were muted early premarket trade ahead of its Aug. 4 earnings report. Morningstar warned that upcoming post-IPO lockup expirations (Aug 6) could create selling pressure while simultaneously boosting the stock's float-adjusted weight inside the QQQ ETF. Outlook Therapeutics (OTLK): Shares rose 7% in early premarket trade following FDA approval of Lytenava for wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), with analysts forecasting up to 290% upside. Oil stocks (USO, BATL, TPET, XOM, CVX, OXY) remained in focus as crude oil prices fell over 6% following the U.S.-Iran military pause. Other tickers trending on Stocktwits at the time of writing included Rigetti Computing (RGTI), Venture Global (VG) and Capricor Therapeutics (CAPR). On the economic front, investors will be watching for the release of durable goods orders and the Dallas Fed manufacturing survey. On the earnings front, Dyne Therapeutics (DYNE), Applied Digital (APLD), and Navitas Semiconductor (NVTS) are among those reporting today. title: 4 Energy Stocks With 20+ Years of Consecutive Dividend Growth - The Globe and Mail
content: The energy sector is known for its volatility, but it still contains some shockingly reliable dividend stocks. Chevron and ExxonMobil are two of the world's largest energy companies and two highly reliable dividend stocks. Enterprise Products Partners and Enbridge sidestep commodity risk and grow their dividends year after year. The geopolitical conflict in the Middle East has once again shown that energy prices are highly volatile. That's the norm for the sector, not the exception, a fact that can make it hard for dividend investors to find attractive energy stocks. But some companies have proven they have what it takes to keep paying through the entire energy cycle. If you are looking for reliable high-yield dividend stocks, Chevron(NYSE: CVX), ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM), Enterprise Products Partners(NYSE: EPD), and Enbridge(NYSE: ENB) all deserve a deep dive. The shortest dividend streak on this list is 27 years! Where to invest $1,000 right now? Our analyst team just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks to buy right now, when you join Stock Advisor. See the stocks » Chevron and Exxon are two of the world's largest energy companies. They are also highly reliable dividend stocks, with decades worth of annual dividend increases behind each one. Exxon's streak is a bit longer at 43 years, but Chevron's 38-year streak is hard to complain about. Right now, Chevron has the higher yield at 3.7%, while Exxon still offers a well-above-market 2.7% yield. The big story here, however, is the businesses that back those yields and dividend streaks. Chevron and Exxon are both integrated energy companies, which means they provide investors exposure to the entire energy value chain, from the upstream (energy production) to the midstream (pipelines) to the downstream (chemical and refining). Their upstream operations have the biggest impact on financial results, but the midstream and downstream exposure helps to soften the large performance swings that often happen in the upstream. Meanwhile, both companies operate in a very conservative fiscal manner. That is highlighted by their peer-leading debt-to-equity ratios of 0.2x for Exxon and 0.25x for Chevron. This allows both companies to lean on their balance sheets during energy market downturns, enabling them to continue supporting their businesses and dividends. And that will allow dividend lovers to sleep well at night knowing that their dividend checks will keep rolling in. The upstream and the downstream are both volatile, but the midstream tends to be rather boring. This is where both Enterprise and Enbridge operate, each owning giant North American energy infrastructure systems. They charge fees for the use of their assets, so the price of the commodities being moved isn't all that important to their financial results. The benefit of this is clear in their dividend track records. Enterprise, a master limited partnership (MLP), has increased its distribution for 27 years, which is the shortest streak on this list, but basically as long as it has been public. Enbridge's dividend streak is 31 years in Canadian dollars. But what's really notable is their yields: Enterprise's is an ultra-high 5.7%, and Enbridge's is not far behind at 5%. There is one caveat here. The yields these midstream giants offer will likely make up a large portion of an investor's return over time. They are, at best, slow-growing and steady giants. Dividend hikes are likely to edge out inflation over time, but not by much. So these are most appropriate for investors looking to maximize the passive income they generate today. The on-again/off-again conflict in the Middle East has again shown that energy is a volatile sector. However, it has also shown how important energy is to the normal functioning of the global economy. Most investors should have some energy exposure in their portfolios. If you are a dividend lover, Chevron, Exxon, Enterprise, and Enbridge are four very strong options to consider given their impressive dividend histories. Intel’s turnaround is closely tied to its foundry business, which recently bagged new marquee customers such as Apple and Tesla. The revenue expansion was largely driven by Intel’s data center operations, where sales soared 59% last quarter to $6.3 billion. RTX’s Q2 revenue and earnings grew at a double-digit pace across its three major businesses: Collins Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney, and Raytheon. The company benefited from rising demand in both commercial aviation and defense markets, helping it deliver results that exceeded Wall Street expectations. RTX generated $2.9 billion in free cash flow during Q2, helped by $3.55 billion in operating cash flow. The company’s backlog surged to a record $289 billion, up 22% year-on-year, including $170 billion in commercial orders and $119 billion in defense contracts. RTX also added $43 billion in new bookings. The company raised its 2026 forecast, seeing revenue of $95 billion to $96 billion, compared with the prior estimate of $92.5 billion to $93.5 billion. RTX stock rose 0.3% overnight, ahead of Friday. The stock has gained 8% so far this week. “Raytheon booked nearly $20 billion of awards, resulting in a book-to-bill in Q2 of 2.4. These bookings included over $5 billion of GEM-T Patriot effectors driven by international customers and our first domestic GEM-T production order in over 30 years. Raytheon's bookings also included over $4 billion of classified and confidential awards as well as $1.8 billion for AMRAAM,” said RTX CEO Christopher Calio during the Q2 earnings call. Lockheed Martin posted a strong Q2 2026 performance, with higher revenue, improved profits, and $65 billion in new orders, helping the company recover from prior-year program losses and strengthening its future growth outlook. The company also generated $2.9 billion in free cash flow, supported by $3.2 billion in operating cash flow. This represented a strong rebound from the $150 million cash outflow reported in last year’s Q2. Lockheed Martin’s total backlog climbed to a record $230 billion, helped by major contracts such as expanded THAAD interceptor production and a $10.5 billion logistics agreement with U.S. Special Operations Command. “These awards are less about any single program than about what they were building in aggregate. Together, they strengthen the nation's production base, adding resilience along with more manufacturing capacity, more sources of supply and greater surge capability, all at a time when these very attributes have become a strategic imperative for the country,” said Lockheed’s CEO, James Taiclet, at the Q2 earnings call. Lockheed Martin stock edged 0.2% lower overnight, heading into Friday. The stock has climbed over 11% so far this week. The U.S. defense industry is entering a period of heightened investor interest following the House passage of a proposed $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027 on Wednesday. The legislation reinforces expectations that military funding will remain a durable priority despite broader debates over federal spending. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around RTX remained in ‘extremely bullish’ territory. Sentiment around LMT improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ territory the previous day. A user said, “Lockheed $LMT – co-manufacturer of F22 Raptor - Stock Soars. Defense Is a Bipartisan Issue.” Another user said, “It hasn't been a great year since February for this sector, but now there is new funding coming in and other factors -- this sector is going to see some love.” So far this year, RTX and LMT stocks have gained 14% and 17%, respectively. (SEZL) is headed for its worst weekly decline since March this year, but it barely puts a dent in the company’s 2026 performance. The PayPal Holdings (PYPL) rival’s shares are down about 9% this week but have soared by over 150% year-to-date. Meanwhile, PYPL stock is down about 3.5% in the same time. Sezzle has been one of the market's top-performing fintech stocks in 2026, backed by strong financial results and improving profitability. In the first quarter, the company beat Wall Street expectations with earnings per share of $1.43 on revenue of $135.5 million, up 29.2% year over year. Management also raised its full-year adjusted net income guidance to $180 million and projected 30% to 35% revenue growth for 2026, reinforcing confidence in the company's growth trajectory. Meanwhile, user growth and engagement also stayed strong through the year. Active subscribers surged 48.4% in Q1 year-on-year to 714,000, while Monthly On-Demand Users and Subscribers rose 34.8% to 887,000. Active consumers increased 13.6% to 3.1 million. Customer engagement also strengthened, with average quarterly purchase frequency reaching a record 7.1 transactions per user, up from 6.1 a year earlier. Repeat customers accounted for 97% of all platform orders, total transactions climbed 35.8% to 9.9 million and Gross Merchandise Volume went up by 37.3% to $1.1 billion. Meanwhile, PYPL stock’s 12-month average price target of $52.68 implies a downside of about 6% from its last close. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. T-Mobile US Inc. (TMUS) stock is headed toward its worst week in six years after mixed fiscal second-quarter (Q2) results, yet Goldman Sachs reiterated its ‘Buy’ rating, citing improving cash flow and 35% upside potential. T-Mobile stock fell over 10% on Thursday as investors looked past better-than-expected Q2 earnings and a higher full-year cash flow forecast, instead worrying that higher-priced plans could slow subscriber growth in the coming months. Goldman Sachs increased its price target for T-Mobile to $230 from $224 while citing continued operational strength and growth opportunities, implying a 35% upside to the stock’s last price. T-Mobile added 277,000 postpaid accounts during Q2, reflecting healthy demand across both mobile phone and broadband services. Goldman Sachs said the company continues to show solid customer momentum, though it expects account additions to moderate to roughly 250,000 in Q3 as some customers react to recent pricing changes. Goldman Sachs said investors may be concerned about T-Mobile’s unchanged 2026 forecast and weaker Q3 expectations, but the firm remains positive on the company’s future growth prospects, citing higher revenue per customer and greater room to add subscribers. Speaking during the Q2 earnings call, T-Mobile US CFO Peter Osvaldik reassured investors that it still expects healthy customer growth for the full year, even as he acknowledged that changes to its pricing strategy will likely weigh on subscriber additions during Q3. “As part of our full year plan and guidance, we anticipated our Q3 rate plan modernization would result in a temporary elevated account churn profile and expect Q3 net postpaid account additions to be approximately 250,000.” Osvaldik said that the expected increase in churn should have a smaller effect on postpaid phone customers because the pricing changes are primarily concentrated among accounts with fewer wireless lines. That distinction suggests the company expects its larger customer relationships to remain relatively stable throughout the transition. He added that the company continues to expect postpaid net account additions of between 950,000 and 1.05 million for 2026. Management said the forecast reflects confidence in the underlying strength of the business despite near-term headwinds tied to its pricing changes. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock jumped to ‘bullish’ from ‘bearish’ territory the previous day, with a 450% increase in message volume over the past week. The telecom giants are facing a tight market, shaped by fixed wireless expansion, aggressive fiber footprints, and AI-driven cost controls. Additionally, SpaceX’s (SPCX) aggressive push into the communications sector by transforming Starlink into a comprehensive telecom platform is adding additional pressure. The New York-based American telecommunications giant is expected to post about a 2% increase in Q2 revenue expected to $35.11 billion from $34.5 billion in the previous comparable quarter, according to Fiscal.ai data. Meanwhile, earnings per share are expected to grow about 4% from $1.22 to $1.27 in the quarter. Verizon trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 8.8x, comparatively lower than AT&T Inc.’s (T) 9.5x multiple and T-Mobile US Inc.’s (TMUS) 13.7x. However, Charter’s forward P/E ratio is significantly lower, trading at a multiple of 2.9x. Despite Verizon’s lower valuation multiple, some Wall Street analysts are wary of the company’s strategy, believing that aggressive cost-cutting alone may not be enough to reignite growth. Earlier this month, reports suggested that Verizon is cutting about 3,000 positions at its corporate-owned retail stores by transitioning 274 locations to independent ownership. Meanwhile, SpaceX’s plans to transform Starlink into a mainstream consumer mobile service is also adding additional pressure. Wall Street analysts are on the fence about Verizon, with 15 out of 26 analysts covering the stock rating it a ‘Hold,’ as per latest data from Koyfin. The rest rate it a ‘Buy.’ However, the average 12-month price target of $51.12 implies an upside of about 16.66% from the stock’s last close. Charter is expected to post about a 2% decline in Q2 revenue from $13.766 billion in 2025 to $13.51 billion this quarter, as per Fiscal.ai data. However, analysts expect an increase of about 13% in earnings per share in the quarter, forecast to come in at $10.41 versus $9.18 in the previous comparable quarter. Meanwhile, reports from last month suggested that Charter has held discussions with Elon Musk's aerospace company over a potential consumer mobile partnership. The talks reportedly involve Charter routing a portion of SpaceX's mobile traffic through its terrestrial broadband network, though neither company has confirmed the discussions so far. Wall Street analysts have a 12-month average price target of $210.32 on CHTR shares, implying an upside of more than 66% from its last close. Of the 21 analysts covering the stock, only five have a ‘Buy’ rating, while 11 have a ‘Hold’ rating on the company. The rest rate it ‘Sell’ or lower. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around VZ stock was ‘bearish’ at the time of writing as message volumes climbed more than 35% in the past 24 hours. Meanwhile, retail sentiment around CHTR stock was also ‘bearish’ amid a 90% increase in message volumes. Both tickers were trending on Stocktwits at the time of writing. One user said, “$VZ It's gonna be a good day tomorrow!” Another user said, “$VZ $TMUS down -9.60% despite a neutral good earnings. $VZ will follow - good position building opportunity tomorrow.  Happy Friday is might be.” A third user said, “$CHTR It will take a few quarters but I think the turn around starts now. Cable is not going away for a while and the enhancements to existing infrastructure will get the company through a few more years until they start thinking more seriously about fiber. Plus the rural expansion makes them an attractive partner to sat companies or a good potential merger candidate for other telcos.” VZ stock has gained about 8% in 2026, while CHTR stock has declined more than 39%.
